one_liner: Go float32/float64/bool vector library with AVX2+FMA assembly kernels, against its own pure-Go loops.
what_it_does: vek is a NumPy-style set of vector functions on plain Go slices: arithmetic, sums and quantiles, dot/norm/distance, MatMul and Mat4Mul, sqrt/round/pow, float32-only sin/cos/exp/log, element-wise comparisons that return []bool masks, boolean And/Or/Any/Count/Select, and construction/conversion helpers. Package vek handles float64 and vek32 handles float32. Each function has an allocating form, an _Inplace form and an _Into(dst, ...) form. On amd64 CPUs with AVX2 and FMA, calls go to generated Go assembly; elsewhere (including macOS and ARM64) the same API runs pure-Go loops.
how_it_is_fast: Most kernels are the same plain C++ loops as the Go fallback, auto-vectorized by Clang with -Ofast -mfma -mavx2 -funroll-loops, then translated into Go assembly through avo with the repo's asm2avo.py. Exp, Log, Pow, Sin and Cos come from Agner Fog's Vector Class Library (vectormath_exp.h), as 8-lane float32 or 4-lane float64 polynomial approximations. Two things the Go compiler will not do account for most of the gain. -Ofast lets Clang reassociate reductions into several vector accumulators (Sum is a serial dependency chain in Go), and if-conversion turns branchy scalar code (&&, if y > x) into branchless blends.
when_to_use: Go services on x86-64 servers with AVX2 and FMA (Haswell or Zen 1 and later) that do element-wise float32 math on slices of a few hundred elements or more.
float32 transcendental-heavy work (exp, log, pow, sqrt over 10k to 100k element slices) that can accept VCL approximation error and has no NaN or Inf inputs.
Reductions and scans in Go (Sum, Max, Find, Count, All, Dot), where the scalar loop is latency-bound or branchy.
Mask-style data filtering (comparisons returning []bool, combined with And and Select), much like NumPy boolean indexing.
Small and medium MatMul in pure-Go deployments with no cgo or BLAS; vek.MatMul splits rows across runtime.NumCPU goroutines.
when_not_to_use: Data that can contain NaN or Inf: the kernels are built with -Ofast, so results are undefined. Issue #11 showed Eq and Neq returning wrong counts with acceleration on, and that was documented, not fixed.
ARM64 (Graviton, Apple silicon) or macOS: there are no NEON kernels, the maintainer said in issue #12 (Nov 2025) that none are planned, and acceleration is off by default on darwin.
Very short slices (under about 8 to 16 elements): issue #6 measured Add on [4]float32 at 3.427 ns with SIMD against 2.174 ns in pure Go, a Ryzen 7 7840HS result.
Integer vectors (only float32, float64 and bool are supported; the ints request in issue #13 was closed), and code that needs bit-for-bit agreement with math.Exp, Log or Pow.
Serious dense linear algebra: MatMul is a naive i-k-j loop, not a blocked BLAS kernel, so use gonum with OpenBLAS or MKL for large matrices.

integration.dependencies: github.com/chewxy/math32, github.com/viterin/partial, golang.org/x/exp, golang.org/x/sys (testify for tests only); no cgo
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.19 (go.mod; generics). Builds on Go 1.21 and later only from the Aug 2023 partial v1.1.0 fix onward (issue #4).
integration.platforms: Accelerated on amd64 with AVX2 and FMA, except darwin, where acceleration is off by default. Any other GOARCH or OS falls back to pure Go.
integration.thread_safety: Stateless functions are safe to call concurrently on disjoint slices. SetAcceleration writes a global flag and is documented 'Not thread safe'. _Inplace and _Into destinations must not overlap the other arguments.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it replaces hand-written Go loops over []float32 or []float64 with function calls of the same semantics, apart from fast-math precision and NaN or Inf behaviour. It is not a drop-in for math.Exp, math.Log or math.Pow results.

gotchas: Harness flaw in the transcendental rows: BenchmarkExpLog, BenchmarkPow and BenchmarkSqrt draw inputs from Random(), which is rand.NormFloat64()*100. About half of the Log, Sqrt and Pow inputs are negative, which gives NaN; Pow uses non-integer exponents in [-10,10]. About 38% of the Exp inputs have |x| > 88.7, which overflows to +Inf or underflows to 0 or a denormal. The README itself calls that regime undefined for the SIMD path. TestExpLog checks Exp only on [-10,10]. The scalar math32.Exp and math32.Log take data-dependent special-case branches on this input mix (math32.Exp tests float64 overflow limits, so the 88.7 to 709 range goes through its slow Ldexp path). The 22x Exp, 16x Log and 14x Pow numbers therefore come from inputs that are mostly invalid.

Branchy baselines inflate two rows. And_Go is x[i] = x[i] && y[i], a short-circuit branch on random 50% bools, while the C++ kernel computes the bitwise x[i] & y[i]; that gap is the 139x. Maximum_Go is if y[i] > x[i] on random normal data, about 5.4 ns per element at 100k against 0.58 ns for Add (derived from page data), so the 8x mostly measures branch mispredictions.

The README's 1k column for Add, Mul, Abs, Round, Sqrt, Pow, Exp, Log, Maximum, Lt and And, and its p=1 MatMul rows, cannot be produced by the committed go test command. Those benchmarks loop over sizes[3:] (10k and 100k only, unchanged since the initial commit ff9d7ac), and BenchmarkMatMul uses only p of 100 or 1000. The README also does not say whether its MatMul rows are the serial or the goroutine-parallel variant. The p=1k SIMD rows imply about 96 GFLOP/s for f64 and 191 GFLOP/s for f32 (derived from page data), more than one core can reach with this i-k-j loop, so they are almost certainly the parallel paths.

Correctness tests only cover lengths 1 to 200 (size = 1 + i/5), so the unrolled main loops that start past 256 elements are exercised only by benchmarks that never check results. That is how the Any() bug (stale RAX returned for len > 256 with len % 32 > 0) survived from 2022 until an outside PR fixed it in Aug 2025 (commit 0ce8425).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick vek over kelindar/simd or tphakala/simd when you want one NumPy-like float32/float64 API that also covers transcendental functions, boolean masks with Select, and MatMul; kelindar/simd's published tables cover integer element types (uint8/uint16/uint32), which vek does not support. Prefer a sibling if you need non-x86 acceleration or strict IEEE results, which vek does not provide.
verified_claims_summary: These are first-party go test benchmark numbers comparing each AVX2 kernel with the library's own pure-Go loop, on an unstated x86-64 CPU, Go version and run count (README table, probably from 2022). Examples at 100k elements: vek32.Sum 65,007 ns against 3,191 ns (20x), vek32.Exp 22x, vek.Add 2x, vek32.Add 6x. The largest ratios (And 139x, Exp 22x, Log 16x, Maximum 8x) come from branchy scalar baselines or from NaN and Inf-producing inputs, not from typical data.
status_note: Stale but MIT-licensed and small (19 commits, 204 stars). The last code fix was the Aug 2025 Any() patch, and the last commit (Sep 2025) added a README note on fast math. The maintainer still answers issues (Nov 2025) but has ruled out ARM64 SIMD. Dgraph, per cross-references on issue #12, replaced vek with in-tree SIMD distance kernels in 2026.
